rows.title: Dynamic Programming
rows.description: 1D/2D grids, 0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS), and Partition DP.

rows.title: Tries
rows.description: Prefix trees, insert/search/startsWith, counting distinct substrings, and Maximum XOR of two numbers in array.

rows.title: Strings (Basic and Medium)
rows.description: Basic and medium string problems, palindrome checks, anagrams, substring patterns, and Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) matching.

rows.title: Recursion
rows.description: Call stack mental models, generating subsets, combinations, permutations, N-Queens, and Sudoku Solver.

rows.title: Strings (Advanced Algo)
rows.description: Handwritten DSA Notes and Java solutions for Strings (Advanced Algo).

rows.title: Maths
rows.description: Handwritten DSA Notes and Java solutions for Maths.

rows.title: Linked-List
rows.description: Singly, Doubly, fast & slow pointers, Floyd's cycle detection, reverse in K-groups, and LRU Cache design.

rows.title: Bit Manipulation
rows.description: Bitwise AND, OR, XOR, power-of-two tests, Brian Kernighan's count, single number variants, and bitmasking.

rows.title: Greedy Algorithms
rows.description: Activity selection, non-overlapping intervals, Jump Game, fractional knapsack, and shortest job first.

rows.title: Beginner Problems
rows.description: Basic maths, recursion fundamentals, hashing basics, time complexity theory, and Java standard library collections.

rows.title: Sorting
rows.description: Complete comparison and recursive sorting algorithms with visual traces. Selection, Bubble, Insertion, Merge, Quick Sort & Inversion counts.

rows.title: Arrays
rows.description: Easy, Medium and Hard array problems. Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Dutch National Flag, Kadane's Algorithm, and Prefix Sums.

rows.title: Hashing
rows.description: Handwritten DSA Notes and Java solutions for Hashing.

rows.title: Binary Search
rows.description: 1D and 2D binary search, search in rotated sorted arrays, binary search on answer space, and monotonic predicates.

rows.title: Sliding Window / 2 Pointer
rows.description: Constant and dynamic window problems, longest substring without repeating characters, and minimum window substring.

rows.title: Stack / Queues
rows.description: Array/Linked List implementations, monotonic stacks, Next Greater Element, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, and sliding window maximum.

rows.title: Binary Trees
rows.description: Traversals (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, Level order), diameter, LCA, tree serialization, and Maximum Path Sum.

rows.title: Binary Search Trees
rows.description: BST invariants, validation, floor & ceil, node deletion, Kth smallest element, and Two Sum in BST.

rows.title: Heaps
rows.description: Min/Max binary heaps, heapify down in O(N), Top-K Frequent Elements, Merge K Sorted Lists, and Median from Data Stream.

rows.title: Graphs
rows.description: BFS, DFS, cycle detection, topological sort (Kahn's), Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU).

rows.title: Majority Element-I
rows.description: Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the majority element. The majority element is the element that appears more than `⌊n / 2⌋` times. You may assume that the majority element always exists in the array. Solve in O(N) time and O(1) space using Moore's Voting Algorithm.
rows.outputFormat: Return the majority integer element.

examples.explanation: 3 appears 2 times in an array of size 3, which is > 3/2 = 1.5.
2 appears 4 times in an array of size 7, which is > 7/2 = 3.5.

rows.title: Reverse an array 2
rows.description: Reverse an array `nums` recursively using two pointers `l` and `r`: swap `nums[l]` and `nums[r]`, then recurse with `l + 1` and `r - 1` until `l >= r`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the reversed array.

rows.title: Print the matrix in spiral manner
rows.description: Given an `m x n` matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (traversing top row left-to-right, right column top-to-bottom, bottom row right-to-left, and left column bottom-to-top repeatedly).
rows.inputFormat: A 2D integer matrix `matrix` with `m` rows and `n` columns.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of integers containing all elements in clockwise spiral traversal order.
rows.constraints:
m == matrix.length
n == matrix[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 100
-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100

examples.explanation: Traversing the perimeter boundary inwards yields the sequence.

rows.title: Pascal's Triangle I
rows.description: Given row number `r` and column number `c`, return the element present at position `(r, c)` in Pascal's triangle (1-indexed). Note that element at `(r, c)` is given by formula `(r-1) C (c-1)`.
rows.inputFormat: Two positive integers `r` and `c` representing row and column (1-indexed).
rows.outputFormat: Return the integer value at position (r, c) of Pascal's triangle.

examples.explanation: In 5th row of Pascal's triangle [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], the 3rd element is 6.

rows.title: Pascal's Triangle III
rows.description: Given an integer `numRows`, return the first `numRows` of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.
rows.inputFormat: An integer `numRows` representing the number of rows to generate.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of lists of integers representing Pascal's triangle up to `numRows`.

examples.explanation: First 5 rows of Pascal's triangle generated systematically.

rows.title: Pascal's Triangle II
rows.description: Given an integer `rowIndex`, return the `rowIndex`-th (1-indexed or 0-indexed as specified) row of Pascal's triangle in O(N) time and O(1) extra auxiliary space.
rows.inputFormat: An integer `n` representing the desired row of Pascal's triangle.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of integers containing the values of row `n`.

examples.explanation: The 4th row of Pascal's triangle contains 1, 3, 3, 1.
The 5th row of Pascal's triangle contains 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

rows.title: Count Number of Substrings
rows.description: Given a string `s` of lowercase alphabets and an integer `k`, count the number of substrings that contain exactly `k` distinct characters. Solve in O(N) time using helper function `atMostK(s, k) - atMostK(s, k - 1)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the count of substrings with exactly `k` distinct characters.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
1 <= k <= 26
s consists of lowercase English characters.

rows.title: Prime factorisation of a Number
rows.description: Given a number `n`, find all of its prime factors in ascending order. Solve in O(sqrt(N)) time using trial division by 2 and odd numbers up to sqrt(n).
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of prime factors of `n`.

rows.title: Print all primes till N
rows.description: Given an integer `n`, generate and return all prime numbers strictly less than or equal to `n` in sorted order. Implement the Sieve of Eratosthenes to achieve O(N log(log N)) time complexity.
rows.outputFormat: Return a sorted list of all prime numbers <= `n`.

rows.title: Different Ways to Evaluate a Boolean Expression
rows.description: Given a boolean expression with operands `T` and `F`, and operators `&` (AND), `|` (OR), and `^` (XOR). Find the number of ways to parenthesize the expression such that it evaluates to true. Since the answer can be large, return it modulo 1003. Solve in O(N^3) using 3D Partition DP tracking both true ways and false ways for every subsegment `[i, j]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the number of ways to evaluate to true modulo 1003.

examples.explanation: Four distinct parenthesizations evaluate to true.

rows.title: Check if the Number is Armstrong
rows.description: Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it is an Armstrong number (also known as a Narcissistic number), otherwise `false`. An n-digit number is an Armstrong number if the sum of its digits raised to the power `k` (where `k` is total number of digits) equals the original number.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if Armstrong number, else `false`.

rows.title: Count of Prime Numbers till N
rows.description: Given an integer `n`, return the count of prime numbers strictly less than `n`. Solve in O(N log(log N)) using the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
rows.outputFormat: Return the count of primes strictly less than `n`.

examples.explanation: There are 4 prime numbers less than 10, they are 2, 3, 5, 7.

rows.title: Basic Hashing
rows.description: Learn direct addressing and basic hashing: using an array of size 26 for lowercase characters or size `max_val + 1` for numbers to achieve O(1) frequency lookups.
rows.outputFormat: Return frequency counts using direct address hashing.

rows.title: GCD of Two Numbers
rows.description: Given two integers `a` and `b`, calculate their Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) / Highest Common Factor (HCF). Solve in O(log(min(a, b))) time using the Euclidean algorithm: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the GCD as an integer.

examples.explanation: 4 is the largest integer dividing both 20 and 28.

rows.title: Check for Prime Number
rows.description: Given an integer `n`, check whether it is a prime number. A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. Solve in O(sqrt(N)) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if prime, else `false`.

rows.title: Rotate matrix by 90 degrees
rows.description: You are given an `n x n` 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image clockwise by 90 degrees in-place. You have to rotate the image in-place without allocating another 2D matrix (accomplished by transposing the matrix and reversing each row).
rows.outputFormat: Modify the matrix in-place rotated 90 degrees clockwise.

examples.explanation: Rotating 90 degrees clockwise transforms row 1 into column 3, row 2 into column 2, and row 3 into column 1.
The 4x4 matrix is rotated clockwise in place.

rows.title: Kadane's Algorithm
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum. Solve in O(N) time using Kadane's dynamic programming algorithm.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum subarray sum as an integer.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] has the largest sum 6.
The entire array [5, 4, -1, 7, 8] has the largest sum 23.

rows.title: Edit distance
rows.description: Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of operations required to convert `word1` to `word2`. You have the following three operations permitted on a word: Insert a character, Delete a character, Replace a character. Solve in O(M * N) time and O(N) space using Levenshtein distance DP.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum edit distance.
rows.constraints:
0 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500
word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Five operations to transform intention to execution.

rows.title: Largest Odd Number in a String
rows.description: You are given a string `num`, representing a large integer. Return the largest-valued odd integer (as a string) that is a non-empty substring of `num`, or an empty string `""` if no odd integer exists. Scan backwards from the end of the string to find the first odd digit.
rows.outputFormat: Return the largest odd substring prefix.
rows.constraints:
1 <= num.length <= 10^5
num only consists of digits and does not contain any leading zeros.

examples.explanation: The only non-empty substrings are "5", "2", and "52". "5" is the only odd number.
"35427" ends with 7 (odd), so the whole string is the largest odd number.

rows.title: Fibonacci Number
rows.description: The Fibonacci numbers, commonly denoted `F(n)` form a sequence, called the Fibonacci sequence, such that each number is the sum of the two preceding ones, starting from `0` and `1`: `F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2)` for `n > 1`. Given `n`, calculate `F(n)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the n-th Fibonacci number.

rows.title: Recursive Insertion Sort
rows.description:
Given an array of integers `nums`, sort the array using a recursive implementation of Insertion Sort.

Base case: If array size is 1 or less, return immediately. Inductive step: Recursively sort the first n-1 elements, then insert the last element at its correct position in the sorted prefix.
rows.inputFormat: An array of integers nums and its length n.
rows.outputFormat: Return the array sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Recursively sorts [0..n-2], then shifts elements rightwards to insert nums[n-1].
Prefix of size 1 is sorted, then 4 is inserted, then 3, then 2, then 1.

rows.explanation: Recursive Insertion Sort mirrors mathematical induction: base case n<=1, hypothesis that [0..n-2] is sorted, and conclusion that shifts place arr[n-1].

rows.title: Recursive Bubble Sort
rows.description:
Given an array of integers `nums`, sort the array using a recursive implementation of Bubble Sort.

In recursive Bubble Sort, the base case is when the array size is 1 (already sorted). In the recursive step, perform one complete pass of bubble sort to move the largest element to the end of the current subarray, and recursively sort the first n-1 elements.
rows.inputFormat: An array of integers nums and its length n.
rows.outputFormat: Return the array sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Pass 1 moves 8 to index 4. The function then recursively calls itself with array size n-1 (size 4).
Each recursive call fixes one largest element at the current tail position.

rows.explanation: Recursive Bubble Sort converts the outer iteration into a recursion call stack while maintaining the inner pairwise comparison pass.

rows.title: Sum of Array Elements II
rows.description: Given an array of integers `nums`, compute the sum of all elements in the array recursively by adding `nums[index]` to the recursive sum of the remaining array.
rows.outputFormat: Return the sum as an integer.

rows.title: Minimum cost to cut the stick
rows.description: Given a wooden stick of length `n` units. The stick is labelled from `0` to `n`. Given an integer array `cuts` where `cuts[i]` denotes a position you should perform a cut at. You can change the order of the cuts as you wish. The cost of one cut is the length of the stick to be cut. Return the minimum total cost of the cuts. Solve in O(C^3) using Partition DP.
rows.inputFormat: An integer `n` (stick length) and integer array `cuts`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum total cutting cost.
rows.constraints:
2 <= n <= 10^6
1 <= cuts.length <= min(n - 1, 100)
1 <= cuts[i] <= n - 1
All elements in cuts are distinct.

examples.explanation: Cut at 3 (cost 7), then at 1 (cost 3), then 4 (cost 4), then 5 (cost 2). Total = 7 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 16.

rows.title: Pattern 1
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 1 shape containing an N x N square of asterisks.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Pattern 4
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 4 shape containing a right-angled triangle with repeating numbers.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Pattern 9
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 9 shape containing a symmetric star diamond.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Pattern 6
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 6 shape containing an inverted right-angled number triangle.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Largest Element
rows.description: Given an array of integers `nums`, find and return the largest element present in the array. You should solve this problem in O(N) time with O(1) auxiliary space.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum integer value found in `nums`.

examples.explanation: The largest element in the array is 10000.
The maximum number among all elements is 90.

rows.title: Second Largest Element
rows.description: Given an array of integers `nums`, find the second largest distinct element in the array. If no second largest distinct element exists (e.g. all elements are equal or length is less than 2), return -1. Strive to solve this in a single traversal (O(N) time) without sorting.
rows.outputFormat: Return the second largest distinct integer, or -1 if it does not exist.

examples.explanation: The largest element is 35 and the second largest distinct element is 34.
All elements are equal, so no second largest distinct element exists.

rows.title: Maximum Consecutive Ones
rows.description: Given a binary array `nums`, return the maximum number of consecutive `1`s appearing consecutively in the array.
rows.inputFormat: A binary integer array `nums` containing only 0s and 1s.
rows.outputFormat: Return an integer representing the maximum count of consecutive 1s.

examples.explanation: The first two digits or the last three digits are consecutive 1s. The maximum number of consecutive 1s is 3.
The maximum sequence of 1s has length 2.

rows.title: Learn Python
rows.description: Master foundational Python programming: dynamic typing, indentation, input parsing via `input().split()`, list comprehensions, slicing `arr[::-1]`, dictionaries, sets, and functions.
rows.outputFormat: Formatted console output.

examples.output: Parses a space-separated line into a list of integers.

examples.explanation: String reversal using Python slice step.

rows.title: Partition Array for Maximum Sum
rows.description: Given an integer array `arr`, partition the array into (contiguous) subarrays of length at most `k`. After partitioning, each subarray has their values changed to become the maximum value of that subarray. Return the largest sum of the given array after partitioning. Solve in O(N * K) time using Front Partition DP.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum partitioned sum.

rows.title: First and last occurrence
rows.description: Given an array of integers `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, find the starting and ending position of a given `target` value. If `target` is not found in the array, return `[-1, -1]`. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity using two binary searches.
rows.inputFormat: A sorted integer array `nums` and target integer `target`.
rows.outputFormat: Return `[firstIndex, lastIndex]`.
rows.constraints:
0 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^9 <= nums[i], target <= 10^9
nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Target 8 appears first at index 3 and last at index 4.
Target 6 is not in the array.

rows.title: Pattern 16
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 16 shape containing an alphabet triangle with repeating letters.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Count Occurrences in a Sorted Array
rows.description: Given a sorted array `nums` of `n` integers and an integer `target`, count the number of occurrences of `target` in the array. Solve in O(log n) time by finding first and last occurrences via binary search and taking `last - first + 1`.
rows.inputFormat: A sorted integer array `nums` and target integer `target`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the count of occurrences of `target` in `nums`.

examples.explanation: 4 does not appear in the array.

rows.title: Find square root of a number
rows.description: Given a non-negative integer `n`, compute and return the integer square root of `n` (`floor(sqrt(n))`). The return type should be an integer, and since we need floor, the decimal digits are truncated. Do not use any built-in exponent or sqrt functions. Solve in O(log n) time using binary search on answer space `[1, n]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the integer floor of the square root of `n`.

examples.explanation: The square root of 8 is 2.82842..., and since the decimal part is truncated, 2 is returned.

rows.title: Find minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
rows.description: Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in ascending order with unique elements is rotated between 1 and `n` times. Given the sorted rotated array `nums` of unique elements, return the minimum element of this array. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `nums` of unique elements sorted and rotated.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum integer element in `nums`.
rows.constraints:
n == nums.length
1 <= n <= 5000
-5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000
All values are unique.

examples.explanation: The original array was [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] rotated 3 times. The minimum is 1.

rows.title: Search in rotated sorted array-II
rows.description: There is an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order (not necessarily distinct values). Given the rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `nums`, or `false` if it is not in `nums`. Handle duplicates where `nums[low] == nums[mid] == nums[high]` by trimming search boundaries.
rows.inputFormat: A rotated sorted array `nums` that may contain duplicate values, and integer `target`.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if target exists, else `false`.

rows.title: Count Good Numbers
rows.description: A digit string is good if the digits (0-indexed) at even indices are even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) and the digits at odd indices are prime (2, 3, 5, 7). Given an integer `n`, return the total number of good digit strings of length `n`. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7. Solve in O(log n) time using binary exponentiation.
rows.outputFormat: Return the count of good digit strings modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: Good numbers of length 1: "0", "2", "4", "6", "8" (5 even digits).
Even indices: 5 choices each (indices 0, 2). Odd indices: 4 choices each (indices 1, 3). Total = 5 * 4 * 5 * 4 = 400.

rows.title: Word Break
rows.description: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. Note that the same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times in the segmentation. Solve in O(N^2) time using dynamic programming.
rows.inputFormat: A string `s` and a list of strings `wordDict`.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if segmentable, else `false`.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 300
1 <= wordDict.length <= 1000
1 <= wordDict[i].length <= 20
All words lowercase.

rows.title: String to Integer (atoi)
rows.description: Implement the `myAtoi(string s)` function, which converts a string to a 32-bit signed integer. The algorithm must: 1. Ignore leading whitespace. 2. Check for optional '+' or '-' sign. 3. Read subsequent digits until a non-digit character is encountered. 4. Clamp the integer within 32-bit signed integer range `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the parsed 32-bit signed integer value.
rows.constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 200
s consists of English letters, digits, ' ', '+', '-', and '.'.

examples.explanation: Leading spaces ignored, '-' indicates negative, digits '042' parsed as 42.

rows.title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses
rows.description: Given a valid parentheses string `s`, return the nesting depth of `s`. The nesting depth is the maximum number of open parentheses that are nested inside one another without being closed.
rows.inputFormat: A string `s` containing characters, digits, and parentheses.
rows.outputFormat: Return an integer representing the maximum nesting depth.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 100
s consists of digits 0-9 and characters '+', '-', '*', '/', '(', and ')'.
s is guaranteed to be a valid parentheses string.

examples.explanation: Digit 8 is inside 3 nested pairs of parentheses.

rows.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
rows.description: Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s`. Solve in O(N^2) time with O(1) space by expanding around potential centers (both odd and even centers), or in O(N) time using Manacher's Algorithm.
rows.outputFormat: Return the longest palindromic substring.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000
s consists of only digits and English letters.

rows.title: Generate Parentheses
rows.description: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses using backtracking. A combination is well-formed if an opening bracket is always available before a closing bracket and total open brackets count equals `n`.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of all unique well-formed parentheses strings.

examples.explanation: All 5 valid combinations of 3 parenthesis pairs.

rows.title: Power Set
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order. Solve using recursion / backtracking or bit manipulation.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `nums` of unique elements.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of all subsets.
rows.constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
All elements are unique.

rows.title: Sum of Beauty of All Substrings
rows.description: The beauty of a string is the difference in frequencies between the most frequent and least frequent characters (ignoring characters with frequency 0). Given a string `s`, return the sum of beauty of all of its substrings.
rows.inputFormat: A string `s` of lowercase English letters.
rows.outputFormat: Return an integer representing the sum of beauty of all substrings.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 500
s consists of only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The substrings with non-zero beauty are ["aab", "aabc", "aabcb", "abcb", "bcb"], each with beauty 1. Sum = 5.
Total sum of beauties across all substrings is 17.

rows.title: Reverse a Stack
rows.description: You are given a stack `St`. You have to reverse the stack using recursion, without using any extra loop (no while or for loops) and without using any other auxiliary data structures.
rows.outputFormat: Reverse the stack in-place using recursion.

examples.explanation: The order of elements in stack is completely reversed.

rows.title: Wildcard matching
rows.description: Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement wildcard pattern matching with support for `'?'` (matches any single character) and `'*'` (matches any sequence of characters, including empty sequence). The matching should cover the entire input string. Solve in O(M * N) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if match, else `false`.
rows.constraints:
0 <= s.length, p.length <= 2000
s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '?' or '*'.

examples.explanation: '?' matches 'c', but the second letter is 'a' not 'b'.

rows.title: Insertion in Linked List
rows.description: Understand the fundamental insertion operations in a Singly Linked List: inserting at head (O(1)), inserting at tail (O(N) or O(1) with tail pointer), and inserting at the k-th position (O(K)).
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a linked list, new value `val`, and insertion target.
rows.outputFormat: Return the updated head of the linked list.

rows.title: Introduction to Singly LinkedList
rows.description: Learn the fundamentals of a Singly Linked List: node structure (`data` and `next` pointer), heap allocation, dereferencing, and converting an array into a linked list in O(N) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return the `head` pointer of the constructed linked list.

examples.explanation: Nodes are chained sequentially from index 0 to n-1.

rows.title: Insertion at the tail of Linked List
rows.description: Given the `head` of a linked list and an integer `val`, insert a new node with value `val` at the end (tail) of the linked list and return the head.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a linked list and an integer `val`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the linked list.

rows.title: Deletion in Linked List
rows.description: Learn core deletion mechanics in a Singly Linked List: deleting the head node, deleting the tail node, and deleting by position or value in O(1) to O(N) time while preventing memory leaks and handling null pointers.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a singly linked list and deletion command.
rows.outputFormat: Return the updated head of the linked list.

examples.explanation: Head node deleted, new head is 10.

rows.title: Insertion at the Kth position of Linked List
rows.description: Given the `head` of a linked list, an integer `val`, and a position `k` (1-indexed), insert a new node with value `val` at position `k` and return the head.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a linked list, integer `val`, and integer `k`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the modified linked list.

rows.title: Deletion in Doubly LL
rows.description: Master deletion operations in a Doubly Linked List: unlinking head, unlinking tail, and removing a node at position k by adjusting both `node.prev.next` and `node.next.prev` in O(1) time.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a DLL and deletion instruction.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the updated DLL.

rows.title: Matrix chain multiplication
rows.description: Given a sequence of matrices, find the most efficient way to multiply these matrices together. The problem is not actually to perform the multiplications, but merely to decide in what order to perform the multiplications. Given array `arr[]` where matrix `i` has dimensions `arr[i-1] x arr[i]`, find minimum scalar multiplications. Solve in O(N^3) using Partition DP: `dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j])`.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `arr` of matrix dimensions.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum scalar multiplications as an integer.

rows.title: Check if LL is palindrome or not
rows.description: Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return `true` if it is a palindrome or `false` otherwise. Solve in O(N) time and O(1) space: 1. Find the middle node using slow/fast pointers. 2. Reverse the second half of the list. 3. Compare values of first half and second half.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a singly linked list.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if palindrome, else `false`.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10^5].
0 <= Node.val <= 9

examples.explanation: List reads the same forward and backward.

rows.title: Delete the middle node in LL
rows.description: You are given the `head` of a linked list. Delete the middle node, and return the `head` of the modified linked list. For a list of size `n`, the 0-indexed middle node is at `⌊n / 2⌋`. Solve in O(N) time and O(1) space using two pointers.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head after deleting the middle node.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10^5].
1 <= Node.val <= 10^5

examples.explanation: Middle node with value 7 (index 3) is deleted.

rows.title: Find Middle of Linked List
rows.description: Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node. Solve in one pass using Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm (`slow` moves 1 step, `fast` moves 2 steps).
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a singly linked list.
rows.outputFormat: Return the middle `TreeNode`.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 100].
1 <= Node.val <= 100

examples.explanation: Since the list has two middle nodes with values 3 and 4, we return the second one.

rows.title: Remove duplicates from sorted DLL
rows.description: Given a doubly linked list of `n` nodes which is sorted in non-decreasing order, remove all duplicate nodes from the DLL in-place such that each unique value appears only once. Solve in O(N) time and O(1) space.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a sorted doubly linked list.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the DLL with duplicates removed.

rows.title: Sort LL
rows.description: Given the `head` of a linked list, return the list after sorting it in ascending order. Solve in O(N log N) time and O(log N) stack space using Merge Sort on Linked List.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of an unsorted linked list.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the sorted linked list.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 5 * 10^4].
-10^5 <= Node.val <= 10^5

rows.title: Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL
rows.description: Given the `head` of a doubly linked list and a key `k`, delete all occurrences of `k` from the doubly linked list and return the head of the modified list in O(N) time and O(1) space.
rows.inputFormat: The `head` of a DLL and integer `k`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the DLL after deleting all instances of `k`.

rows.title: Minimum insertions or deletions to convert string A to B
rows.description: Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of steps required to make `word1` and `word2` the same. In each step, you can delete or insert one character. Formula: `(len(word1) - LCS) + (len(word2) - LCS)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum operations count.
rows.constraints:
1 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500
word1 and word2 consist of only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Delete 's' from "sea" to get "ea", insert 't' to get "eat".

rows.title: Swap Two Numbers
rows.description: Given two numbers `a` and `b`, swap their values without using a third temporary variable. Use the bitwise XOR property: `a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the swapped pair `[a, b]`.

rows.title: Single Number - II
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums` where every element appears three times except for one, which appears exactly once. Find the single element and return it. You must implement a solution with O(N) runtime complexity and O(1) extra space using bit counters or bit manipulation (`ones` and `twos`).
rows.outputFormat: Return the integer that appears once.
rows.constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4
-2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1
Every element appears three times except one.

rows.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
rows.description: Given an array of intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping. Greedily sort intervals by end time.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum number of interval removals.

examples.explanation: [1, 3] can be removed and the rest of the intervals are non-overlapping.
You need to remove two [1, 2] to make the rest non-overlapping.

rows.title: Jump Game - I
rows.description: You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. Return `true` if you can reach the last index, or `false` otherwise. Solve in O(N) time by greedily tracking the maximum reachable index.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if the last index is reachable, else `false`.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
You will always arrive at index 3 no matter what. Its maximum jump length is 0, making reaching the end impossible.

rows.title: Burst balloons
rows.description: You are given `n` balloons, indexed from `0` to `n - 1`. Each balloon is painted with a number on it represented by an array `nums`. You are asked to burst all the balloons. If you burst balloon `i` you will get `nums[i - 1] * nums[i] * nums[i + 1]` coins. If `i - 1` or `i + 1` goes out of bounds of the array, then treat it as if there is a balloon with a 1 painted on it. Return the maximum coins you can collect. Solve using reverse Partition DP in O(N^3) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum coins collectable.

rows.title: Infix to Prefix Conversion
rows.description: Given an infix expression `s`, convert it into its equivalent Prefix expression using operator precedence. Algorithm: reverse string, swap `(` with `)`, compute postfix, and reverse the result.
rows.outputFormat: Return the equivalent prefix string.

examples.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition.

rows.title: Implementation using different DS
rows.description: Understand the core abstractions of LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) Stacks and FIFO (First-In-First-Out) Queues. Learn their memory models, asymptotic complexities for `push()`, `pop()`, `peek()`, and `isEmpty()`, and how underlying contiguous arrays vs. dynamically allocated linked nodes affect cache locality and reallocation overhead.
rows.inputFormat: A sequence of push, pop, and top operations.
rows.outputFormat: Return results of queries demonstrating LIFO / FIFO state.

examples.explanation: LIFO stack returns 2 on pop and leaves 1 at top.

rows.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion
rows.description: Given an infix expression `s` containing operands and operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`, `(`, `)`), convert it to its equivalent Postfix expression using an operator stack and operator precedence rules.
rows.outputFormat: Return the equivalent postfix string.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
s contains valid infix expression.

examples.explanation: Standard infix converted to postfix notation.

rows.title: Implement stack using Linkedlist
rows.description: Implement a Stack data structure using a Singly Linked List where nodes contain `data` and `next` pointer. Insertions and deletions occur at the head of the linked list in O(1) time.
rows.inputFormat: A sequence of operations: push(x) and pop().
rows.outputFormat: Return array of values returned by pop operations.

examples.explanation: 20 was at head; after pop, 10 is at head.

rows.title: Prefix to Infix Conversion
rows.description: Given a Prefix expression `s`, convert it to an Infix expression with appropriate parentheses. Traverse from right to left, pushing operands onto the stack and combining when an operator is encountered.
rows.outputFormat: Return the infix expression string with parentheses.

examples.explanation: Converted to valid parenthesized infix form.

rows.title: Implement queue using Linkedlist
rows.description: Implement a Queue data structure using a Singly Linked List with `front` and `rear` pointers. `push(x)` appends a new node at `rear`, and `pop()` removes the node at `front` in O(1) time.
rows.inputFormat: A sequence of operations: push(x) and pop().
rows.outputFormat: Return array of popped values.

rows.title: Number of Greater Elements to the Right
rows.description: Given an array of `n` integers and `q` queries, each containing an index. For each query, return the count of elements that are strictly greater than `arr[query_index]` and lie to its right in the array.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `arr` of size `n`, an integer `q`, and an array of `indices`.
rows.outputFormat: Return an array of query answers.

examples.explanation: To right of index 0 (val 3): 4, 7, 5, 8, 10, 6 (6 elements). To right of index 5 (val 8): 10 (1 element).
No elements to the right of the last index.

rows.title: Maximum path sum
rows.description: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence has an edge connecting them. A node can only appear in the sequence at most once. The path sum is the sum of the node's values in the path. Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum path sum.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 3 * 10^4].
-1000 <= Node.val <= 1000

examples.explanation: The optimal path is 2 -> 1 -> 3 with path sum 2 + 1 + 3 = 6.

rows.title: Introduction
rows.description: Learn the fundamentals of Binary Trees: root node, left and right children, leaf nodes, depth, height, and degrees. Understand types of binary trees: Full, Complete, Perfect, Balanced, and Degenerate trees. Learn tree node representation: `class TreeNode { int val; TreeNode left; TreeNode right; }`.
rows.inputFormat: Conceptual or serialized representation of binary tree nodes.
rows.outputFormat: Return or demonstrate basic tree construction and node counting.

examples.explanation: Binary tree with 5 nodes has root 1, children 2 and 3, and leaves 4 and 5.

rows.title: LFU Cache
rows.description: Design and implement a data structure for a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache. Support `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` in O(1) average time complexity. When capacity is exceeded, invalidate and evict the least frequently used key. If there is a tie, invalidate the least recently used key among them. Maintain a hash map of frequencies to Doubly Linked Lists.
rows.outputFormat: Return results matching LFU cache semantics.
rows.constraints:
1 <= capacity <= 10^4
0 <= key <= 10^5
0 <= value <= 10^9
At most 2 * 10^5 calls.

examples.input: LFUCache(2), put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3), get(2), get(3), put(4, 4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: Key 2 had frequency 1 and was LRU among frequency 1, so it is evicted when key 3 is inserted.

rows.title: Pre, Post, Inorder in one traversal
rows.description: Given a binary tree, print its Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder traversals in a single traversal using one stack of pairs `(TreeNode, state)`. If state is 1: record preorder and increment state; if 2: record inorder and increment; if 3: record postorder and pop.
rows.inputFormat: The `root` node of a binary tree.
rows.outputFormat: Return an object/tuple containing `[preorder, inorder, postorder]` lists.

examples.explanation: All three traversals generated concurrently in one stack pass.

rows.title: Zig Zag or Spiral Traversal
rows.description: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the zigzag level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between). Solve in O(N) using BFS and a boolean flag.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of lists of integers in zigzag level order.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 2000].
-100 <= Node.val <= 100

examples.explanation: Level 0: left to right [3]. Level 1: right to left [20, 9]. Level 2: left to right [15, 7].

rows.title: Rod cutting problem
rows.description: Given a rod of length `N` inches and an array of prices `price` that includes prices of all pieces of size smaller than or equal to `N`. Determine the maximum value obtainable by cutting up the rod and selling the pieces. Unbounded knapsack model where piece size `i` has profit `price[i - 1]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return maximum revenue as an integer.

examples.explanation: Cut into pieces of lengths 2 and 6 for price 5 + 17 = 22.
Cut into 8 pieces of length 1 for 8 * 3 = 24.

rows.title: Count total nodes in a complete BT
rows.description: Given the `root` of a complete binary tree, return the number of the nodes in the tree. According to Wikipedia, every level, except possibly the last, is completely filled, and all nodes in the last level are as far left as possible. Design an algorithm that runs in less than O(N) time (specifically O(log^2 N)) by comparing left and right heights.
rows.inputFormat: The `root` of a complete binary tree.
rows.outputFormat: Return total count of nodes as an integer.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5 * 10^4].
0 <= Node.val <= 5 * 10^4
The tree is guaranteed to be complete.

rows.title: Minimum time taken to burn the BT from a given Node
rows.description: Given a binary tree and a target node `start`. Find the minimum time required to burn the entire binary tree if the target node is set on fire. In 1 unit of time, fire spreads to connected nodes (parent, left child, right child). Solve using radial BFS.
rows.inputFormat: The `root` of a binary tree and integer `start`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum time in seconds/units to burn the tree completely.
rows.constraints:
1 <= nodes <= 10^5
All node values are distinct.

examples.input: root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6, null, null, 7, 8, null, 9, 10, null], start = 8
examples.explanation: The maximum distance from node 8 to any node in the tree is 7 units of time.
At t=1, 1 catches fire; at t=2, 3 catches fire. Total = 2.

rows.title: Vertical Order Traversal
rows.description: Given the `root` of a binary tree, calculate the vertical order traversal of the binary tree. For each node at `(row, col)`, its left child is at `(row + 1, col - 1)` and right is at `(row + 1, col + 1)`. If two nodes have the same row and col, sort them by value. Group results by column from leftmost to rightmost.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of lists of node values ordered vertically by columns.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 1000].
0 <= Node.val <= 1000

examples.explanation: Column -1 has [9]; Column 0 has [3, 15]; Column 1 has [20]; Column 2 has [7].

rows.title: Top View of BT
rows.description: Given a binary tree, print the top view of the binary tree. The top view consists of the set of nodes visible when the tree is viewed from the top. For each vertical column coordinate, only the topmost node is included in the result.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of node values representing the top view from leftmost to rightmost column.

examples.explanation: Nodes 4, 2, 1, 3, 7 are visible from the top.

rows.title: Minimum and Maximum in BST
rows.description: Given a Binary Search Tree, find the minimum and maximum value present in it. In a BST, the leftmost node is the minimum and the rightmost node is the maximum.
rows.outputFormat: Return `[minValue, maxValue]`.

examples.explanation: Leftmost node is 1 and rightmost node is 7.

rows.title: Heaps (Theory Video)
rows.description: Learn the fundamentals of Binary Heaps (Min-Heap and Max-Heap). A binary heap is a Complete Binary Tree represented efficiently as an array: for node at index `i`, left child is at `2*i + 1`, right child is at `2*i + 2`, and parent is at `(i - 1) / 2`. In a Min-Heap, `parent <= children`; in a Max-Heap, `parent >= children`.
rows.outputFormat: Determine heap representation and tree properties.

examples.explanation: Root 10 is smaller than children 20 and 15; 20 is smaller than 30 and 40.
Root 50 is greater than all descendant values.

rows.title: Two sum in BST
rows.description: Given the `root` of a binary search tree and an integer `k`, return `true` if there exist two elements in the BST such that their sum is equal to `k`, or `false` otherwise. Solve in O(N) time and O(h) space using two `BSTIterator` instances: one moving forward (normal inorder) and one moving backward (reverse inorder).
rows.inputFormat: The `root` of a BST and target integer `k`.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if pair exists, else `false`.
rows.constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
-10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4
root is guaranteed to be a valid BST.
-10^5 <= k <= 10^5

rows.title: Convert Min Heap to Max Heap
rows.description: You are given an array representing a Min-Heap. Convert it into a Max-Heap in O(N) time by running Max-Heapify from index `(n - 2) / 2` down to index `0`.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `arr` of size `n` representing a min-heap.
rows.outputFormat: Modify `arr` in-place converting it into a valid max-heap.

rows.title: Build heap from a given Array
rows.description: Given an array of `n` integers, build a Max-Heap from the array in O(N) linear time using bottom-up heapification starting from the last non-leaf node `n/2 - 1` down to index `0`.
rows.inputFormat: An unsorted integer array `nums` of length `n`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the array rearranged as a valid Max-Heap.

rows.title: Design Twitter
rows.description: Design a simplified version of Twitter where users can post tweets, follow/unfollow other users, and view the 10 most recent tweets in their news feed. Implement `postTweet(userId, tweetId)`, `getNewsFeed(userId)` (returning 10 most recent tweets from self and followees using a Max-Heap / PriorityQueue of user tweets), `follow(followerId, followeeId)`, and `unfollow(followerId, followeeId)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return lists of tweet IDs for getNewsFeed queries.
rows.constraints:
1 <= userId, followerId, followeeId <= 500
0 <= tweetId <= 10^4
At most 3 * 10^4 calls.

examples.input: Twitter(), postTweet(1, 5), getNewsFeed(1), follow(1, 2), postTweet(2, 6), getNewsFeed(1), unfollow(1, 2), getNewsFeed(1)
examples.explanation: News feed updates appropriately on tweet and follow actions.

rows.title: Merge K sorted Lists
rows.description: You are given an array of `k` linked-lists lists, each linked-list is sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it. Solve in O(N log K) time using a Min-Heap of size `k` storing the head node of each list.
rows.inputFormat: An array of `k` sorted linked list heads.
rows.outputFormat: Return the head of the single merged sorted linked list.
rows.constraints:
k == lists.length
0 <= k <= 10^4
0 <= total nodes <= 10^4
-10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4

examples.explanation: All lists merged into one sorted linked list.

rows.title: Maximum Sum Combination
rows.description: Given two integer arrays `A` and `B` of size `n` each. A sum combination is made by adding one element from `A` and one element from `B`. Return the `c` largest sum combinations sorted in descending order. Solve in O(C log C) time using a Max-Heap of pairs `(A[i] + B[j], i, j)` after sorting `A` and `B` descending.
rows.inputFormat: Two integer arrays `A` and `B`, and integer `c`.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of `c` integers representing the largest sum combinations.

rows.title: Introduction to Graph
rows.description: Learn the fundamentals of Graph Theory: vertices (nodes), edges (directed vs. undirected, weighted vs. unweighted), degrees, in-degree and out-degree. Understand graph representations in memory: Adjacency Matrix (O(V^2) space) and Adjacency List (O(V + E) space).
rows.inputFormat: Number of vertices `V`, edges `E`, and edge pairs.
rows.outputFormat: Return or construct the adjacency list representation of the graph.

examples.explanation: Adjacency list captures all undirected connections.

rows.title: Word ladder II
rows.description: A transformation sequence from word `beginWord` to word `endWord` using a dictionary `wordList` is a sequence where each adjacent pair differs by one letter. Return all the shortest transformation sequences from `beginWord` to `endWord`, or an empty list if no such sequence exists. Solve using BFS level mapping followed by backtracking DFS from endWord to beginWord.
rows.outputFormat: Return a list of all shortest transformation path lists.
rows.constraints:
1 <= beginWord.length <= 10
endWord.length == beginWord.length
1 <= wordList.length <= 500
All words unique.

examples.explanation: There are two shortest transformation paths of length 5.

rows.title: Network Delay Time
rows.description: You are given a network of `n` nodes, labeled from 1 to `n`. You are also given `times`, a list of travel times as directed edges `times[i] = [u_i, v_i, w_i]`. We will send a signal from a given node `k`. Return the minimum time it takes for all the `n` nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all the `n` nodes to receive the signal, return -1. Solve in O(E log V) using Dijkstra's algorithm.
rows.inputFormat: A list of directed edges `times`, integer `n`, and source node `k`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum time, or -1.

examples.explanation: Signal reaches node 1 at t=1, node 3 at t=1, and node 4 at t=2. Total time = 2.

rows.title: Number of ways to arrive at destination
rows.description: You are in a city that consists of `n` intersections numbered from 0 to `n - 1` with bi-directional roads. Return the number of ways you can arrive at destination `n - 1` in the shortest amount of time. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7. Solve in O(E log V) using modified Dijkstra tracking shortest distances and number of paths.
rows.inputFormat: Integer `n` and 2D array `roads` where `roads[i] = [u, v, time]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the number of shortest paths modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: The 4 paths of shortest distance 7 are: 0-6, 0-4-6, 0-1-2-5-6, 0-1-3-5-6.

rows.title: Minimum multiplications to reach end
rows.description: Given start, end, and an array `arr` of integers. At each step, start is multiplied with any number in the array and then taken modulo 100000. Find the minimum number of steps to reach `end` from `start`. If impossible, return -1. Solve in O(100000 * N) time using BFS on a state graph of size 100000.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `arr`, starting integer `start`, and target integer `end`.
rows.outputFormat: Return minimum multiplications, or -1.

rows.title: Print Shortest Path
rows.description: You are given a weighted undirected graph having `n` vertices numbered from 1 to `n` and `m` edges along with their weights. Find the shortest path from vertex 1 to vertex `n`. If no path exists, return `[-1]`. Otherwise, return the sequence of vertices on the path with path weight sum. Use a `parent[]` array alongside Dijkstra's algorithm.
rows.inputFormat: Integers `n` (vertices), `m` (edges), and edge list `(u, v, weight)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the path array starting with vertex 1 and ending at vertex n (with total weight).

examples.explanation: Total weight of path 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 5 is 1 + 3 + 1 = 5, which is the minimum.

rows.title: Distinct subsequences
rows.description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` which equals `t`. The test cases are generated so that the answer fits on a 64-bit signed integer. Solve in O(M * N) time and O(N) space using 2D DP.
rows.outputFormat: Return the count of distinct subsequences matching `t`.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 1000
s and t consist of English letters.

examples.explanation: There are 3 ways to form "rabbit" by omitting one of the 'b's.

rows.title: Grid unique paths
rows.description: There is a robot on an `m x n` grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner `(0, 0)` and wants to reach the bottom-right corner `(m - 1, n - 1)`. The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. Given the two integers `m` and `n`, return the number of possible unique paths. Solve using 2D DP `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]` in O(m * n) time and O(n) space, or using combinations `(m+n-2) C (m-1)` in O(min(m, n)).
rows.outputFormat: Return the number of unique paths as an integer.

examples.explanation: From (0, 0) to (2, 6) there are 28 unique down/right paths.
Three unique paths: Right->Down->Down, Down->Down->Right, Down->Right->Down.

rows.title: Climbing stairs
rows.description: You are climbing a staircase. It takes `n` steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top? Solve in O(N) time and O(1) space using recurrence: `ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2)`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the number of distinct ways to climb to the top.

examples.explanation: Two ways: 1 step + 1 step, or 2 steps.

rows.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
rows.description: Given an `n x n` array of integers `matrix`, return the minimum sum of any falling path through `matrix`. A falling path starts at any element in the first row and chooses the element in the next row that is either directly below or diagonally left/right. Solve in O(n^2) time and O(n) space using bottom-up DP.
rows.outputFormat: Return the minimum falling path sum.

rows.title: Cherry pickup II
rows.description: You are given a `rows x cols` matrix `grid` representing a field of cherries where `grid[i][j]` represents the number of cherries in that cell. You have two robots: Robot #1 is at `(0, 0)` and Robot #2 is at `(0, cols - 1)`. In each step, both robots move down to row `i + 1` and can shift column by -1, 0, or +1. If both are at the same cell, only one takes the cherries. Return the maximum cherries collected. Solve in O(rows * cols^2) using 3D DP `dp[i][j1][j2]`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the maximum cherries collected by both robots.
rows.constraints:
rows == grid.length
cols == grid[i].length
2 <= rows, cols <= 70
0 <= grid[i][j] <= 100

examples.explanation: Path of robot 1 and 2 maximizes total cherries collected to 24.

rows.title: Unique paths II
rows.description: You are given an `m x n` integer array `obstacleGrid`. There is a robot initially at `(0, 0)`. The robot tries to move to `(m - 1, n - 1)`. It can only move either down or right. An obstacle and space are marked as 1 or 0 respectively in `obstacleGrid`. A path cannot include any square that is an obstacle. Return the number of possible unique paths.
rows.inputFormat: An `m x n` 2D grid containing 0s and 1s.
rows.outputFormat: Return the number of obstacle-free unique paths.
rows.constraints:
m == obstacleGrid.length
n == obstacleGrid[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 100
obstacleGrid[i][j] is 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: There is one obstacle in the middle of the 3x3 grid. Two unique paths reach bottom-right.

rows.title: Longest palindromic subsequence
rows.description: Given a string `s`, find the longest palindromic subsequence's length in `s`. Solve by finding the Longest Common Subsequence between string `s` and its reverse `reverse(s)` in O(N^2) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000

rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Valid Anagram
rows.description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise. An Anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once. Solve in O(N) time using a frequency array of size 26.
rows.outputFormat: Return boolean `true` if anagrams, else `false`.
rows.constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 5 * 10^4
s and t consist of lowercase English letters.

rows.title: Insertion Sort
rows.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, sort the array using the Insertion Sort algorithm.

Insertion Sort works similar to the way you sort playing cards in your hands. Array is virtually split into a sorted and an unsorted part. Values from the unsorted part are picked and placed at the correct position in the sorted part.
rows.outputFormat: Return the array sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Elements before the current index are shifted rightwards if greater than the key to make room.
1 is inserted before 3 giving [1,3,2], then 2 is inserted between 1 and 3 giving [1,2,3].

rows.explanation: Insertion Sort is adaptive: if the input is already sorted, it runs in linear O(N) time with only N-1 comparisons and zero swaps. Default inner sorter in hybrid engines like Timsort.

rows.title: Remove duplicates from sorted array
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same. Return the number of unique elements `k`.
rows.inputFormat: A sorted integer array `nums` in non-decreasing order.
rows.outputFormat: Return integer `k`, the count of unique elements, with the first `k` elements of `nums` holding the unique values.
rows.constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4
-100 <= nums[i] <= 100
nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Your function should return k = 2, with the first two elements of nums being 1 and 2 respectively.
Your function should return k = 5, with the first five elements of nums being 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.

rows.title: Pattern 11
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 11 shape containing a binary triangle alternating 1 and 0.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: Basic Maths
rows.description: Understand foundational mathematical operations in programming: modulo arithmetic, digit extraction using `% 10` and `/ 10`, prime number testing in O(sqrt(N)), Euclidean algorithm for GCD, and counting divisors.
rows.outputFormat: Demonstrate core mathematical evaluations.

rows.title: Reverse an array
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums`, reverse the elements in-place using two pointers (`left` and `right`) in O(N) time and O(1) extra space.
rows.outputFormat: Return the array reversed in-place.

rows.title: Recursion Concepts with Parameters
rows.description: Learn the difference between Parameterized Recursion (accumulating the running result in a parameter down the call stack) and Functional Recursion (returning and combining the result up the call stack upon unwinding).
rows.outputFormat: Compare parameterized vs functional recursive outputs.

examples.input: Parameterized: sum(n, total) -> sum(n - 1, total + n)
examples.output: Returns total directly when n reaches 0.

rows.title: Move Zeros to End
rows.description: Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`s to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. You must do this in-place without making a copy of the array.
rows.outputFormat: Modify the array in-place so all zeros are shifted to the end.

examples.explanation: All non-zero elements [1, 3, 12] maintain their original relative order while all zeros are shifted to the end.
Array contains only zero, so no modification needed.

rows.title: Pattern 13
rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 13 shape containing Floyd's triangle of consecutive increasing numbers.
rows.inputFormat: A single positive integer `N` representing the dimension / height of the pattern.
rows.outputFormat: Print the corresponding pattern to standard output.

rows.title: STL
rows.description: Master the C++ Standard Template Library (STL): sequential containers (`vector`, `deque`, `list`), associative containers (`set`, `map`, `unordered_set`, `unordered_map`), container adapters (`stack`, `queue`, `priority_queue`), and common algorithms (`sort`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `reverse`, `next_permutation`).
rows.outputFormat: Demonstrate sorting and searching using C++ STL algorithms.

examples.explanation: std::sort uses Introsort running in O(N log N) time.
Default C++ priority_queue is a Max-Heap.

rows.title: Factorial of a given number
rows.description: Given a non-negative integer `n`, compute and return `n!` (`n * (n - 1) * ... * 1`). Note that `0! = 1`. Solve iteratively in O(N) time.
rows.outputFormat: Return the factorial value as a long integer.

rows.title: Recursion Theory
rows.description: Learn the principles of recursion: Base Cases (preventing infinite recursion and stack overflow) and Recursive Step (reducing problem size towards the base case). Understand the function call stack, stack frames, local variable allocation, and the flow of control on unwinding.
rows.outputFormat: Demonstrate recursive call stack progression.

examples.explanation: Base case at N+1 unwinds and prints.
Recursion without a base case exhausts the call stack.

rows.title: Reverse a String I
rows.description: Given a string `s`, reverse the string recursively by swapping characters at `i` and `s.length() - 1 - i` until `i >= s.length() / 2`.
rows.outputFormat: Return the reversed string.

rows.title: Rearrange array elements by sign
rows.description: You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of even length consisting of an equal number of positive and negative integers. Rearrange the elements of `nums` such that the modified array follows the pattern: every consecutive pair has opposite signs, it begins with a positive integer, and the relative order of positive and negative integers is preserved.
rows.inputFormat: An integer array `nums` of even length `n` containing equal count of positive and negative integers.
rows.outputFormat: Return the rearranged array starting with positive integer and alternating signs.
rows.constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^5
nums.length is even.
1 <= |nums[i]| <= 10^5
Equal number of positive and negative integers.

examples.explanation: The positive integer 1 must come first, followed by -1.

rows.description: Given an integer `N`, print the Pattern 18 shape containing an alphabet triangle printing characters backwards from N-th letter.

C

D
